long_biography.plain_text:
Sero Shirtmakers made Seymour Shapiro a defining figure in New Haven's post-war garment trade. Born in Brooklyn, he founded the company in 1954 after learning the industry through his father's contract shirtmaking operation. He favoured specialist menswear shops over department stores and built a manufacturing network that eventually supplied thousands of retailers across the United States.

Shapiro's commercial instinct extended beyond production. He developed fabrics, turned the mischievous Scoundrel name into a shirt label, and negotiated a limited trademark licence when Revlon wanted it for a fragrance. Sero expanded into women's clothing and employed a large regional workforce under his leadership. The company became one of the last substantial sewing manufacturers operating in the north-eastern United States.
